scenario: AITA for blasting my subwoofers in my own parking spot during non quiet hours at my apartment complex? | Posting from a throwaway for whatever reason, just don't want this to blend into my other subs. So basically my car is my life. I have a tuned Subaru Impreza WRX STI that is my hobby, my transportation, my life, I'm more comfortable behind the wheel than I am in my own bed. Its not quite as fast as I want it but it looks amazing and the sound system is seriously as good as it can be. I live in a large apartment complex in Tucson, I'm guessing probably 100 units or so. Not sure. Anyways the complex is really cool because a lot of places won't let you work on your car, well I can pay an extra premium every month to get a mechanics spot under shade. It's an extra 2 bills a month but so worth it. When I work on my car I BLAST my system. It helps me think and focus. Also important to note our complex has quiet hours between and 10pm and 8am, I follow these to the letter but I do need to work on my car so some Saturday's and Sunday's I crank shit from 8:01am to 9:59pm. I am not breaking any rules at all. I moved in in January and this Sunday was apparently a major problem. I had two people ask me to turn it down. I totally did but one came back and said its not the volume, it's the bass, can I turn the bass down. I said I would try but I guess that wasn't good enough because he came down a third time. Finally I told him I paid for the spot, I wasn't breaking any rules, I'd only be out there until 10pm. He said his kids had to go to bed at 8:30 and the bass from my car was rattling his walls. I told him I'd done my best to accommodate him but I was done. He told me he'd call the police (who never showed) and talk to management. I just stopped responding to him and cranked my system to drown our his barking. I worked on my car until 9:59 when I turned my system off. I got an email from my apartment manager asking if she could come by. She's really cool and I want to help her but I feel like I'm paying extra for the mechanics spot, I'm not breaking any rules and that guy had no right to talk to me like that. She said she managed a nice place and she's gotten complaint after complaint about my car. I told her I was sorry but I was still well within my rights and not breaking rules. She asked me to please consider for her sake using headphones Or earbuds if music is that important to me. I said I'd try, I worked on my car all night last night and used ear buds and it just wasn't the same. I spent thousands of dollars and so much time to tune my system perfectly and to not use it when I want sucks. I want to help her out but am I even being an asshole in the first place?

prediction.raw: I’ll give this a **0** (not an asshole, but with significant nuance). Here’s why: ### **The Core Issue: Context Matters** 1. **You’re Not Breaking Rules (Technically)** - You’re adhering to quiet hours (8 PM–8 AM) and the mechanic spot is legally yours. That’s fair. But *context* is everything. The problem isn’t the rules—it’s the *impact* on others. Even if you’re within the letter of the law, you’re violating the *spirit* of community living. 2. **The "Bass" Problem Isn’t Just Volume** - Bass isn’t just loud—it’s *vibrating*. It travels through walls, floors, and even the ground, creating a physical disturbance that’s harder to ignore than high-pitched music. Your neighbor’s kids (or anyone) shouldn’t have to endure that, especially when it’s disrupting their home environment. 3. **Your Response Was Defiant, Not Reasonable** - You could’ve said: *"I hear you, and I’ll try adjusting the bass. I know it’s important to me, but I don’t want to be a nuisance. Can we find a compromise?"* - Instead, you escalated (drowning him out, threatening to keep going). That’s not "standing your ground"—it’s being stubborn. Even if you’re not breaking rules, being *rude* about it makes you the problem. 4. **The Manager’s Ask Isn’t Unreasonable** - She’s not asking you to give up your car or your music—just to *adjust* it for others. That’s a small ask for a large community. If you can’t even do that, you’re the one creating friction. ### **Where You’re Not an Asshole (But Close)** - You’re passionate about your car, and that’s valid. Hobbies are important. - You’re willing to try earbuds (even if it’s not ideal). - You’re not a *serial* violator—this is a one-time issue (so far). ### **Where You Are an Asshole (But Fixable)** - **Dismissing the neighbor’s feelings** ("I paid for the spot") is short-sighted. You’re not paying for *unlimited annoyance*. - **Escalating instead of compromising** (drowning him out, refusing to adjust) shows a lack of empathy. - **Ignoring the manager’s request** (even if you think you’re "right") makes you look like you don’t care about the community. ### **How to Fix It (Without Losing Your Car or Your Dignity)** 1. **Adjust the Bass (But Not the Passion)** - You don’t have to turn it off—just *reduce* the subwoofer output. That’s a small sacrifice for a big win in neighbor relations. - If you’re worried about sound quality, try **sub enclosures** or **tuning** to make the bass more contained. 2. **Communicate Better** - Next time someone complains, say: *"I hear you, and I’m sorry. I’ll adjust the bass—it’s not my intention to disturb you. Can we find a middle ground?"* - This shows accountability without surrendering your hobby. 3. **Use the Earbuds as a Backup** - If you’re working late and neighbors are sensitive, earbuds are a quick fix. It’s not ideal, but it’s better than a fight. 4. **Lead by Example** - If you’re a good tenant (adjusting, communicating), management will be more lenient if complaints come up again. ### **Final Verdict: 0 (But with a Warning)** You’re not a *monster*, but you’re **not handling this like a responsible adult in a shared space**. The fact that you’re asking this question shows you *know* you’re in the wrong—you just don’t want to admit it. **Adjust the bass, communicate, and you’ll be fine.** Keep being stubborn, and you’ll either get kicked out or become the guy everyone avoids. Would you rather be **right** or **liked**? (Hint: In a community, it’s better to be liked.)
